title: When you stop, and start again
hookLine: two weeks of all five, then one missed, then none: the deeds most loved are the steady ones, even if small

cards: Ramadan, or a new year, or a hard week, and the prayers come back. Two weeks, all five. Then one gets missed.
Then two. Then the adhan sounds from a phone across the room, there's a sting of guilt, and the prayer still doesn't happen. A few months later, the whole thing starts again.
Underneath sits one quiet question: am I a bad Muslim? Today, what the tradition says to someone stuck in that loop.

teach.b: First, the plain part. Across the major schools, the five daily prayers are a duty, not an extra. This lesson doesn't soften that.
It's about how people get back to them. Aisha, the Prophet's wife, reported a saying that speaks straight to the loop. The Prophet ﷺ was asked which deeds are most loved by Allah.

teach.h: MOST LOVED: THE STEADY ONES, EVEN IF SMALL.
teach.b: The most constant ones, he said, even if small. In Arabic, wa in qall: even if it is little. And when he began something, she added, he kept it up.
Not the heroic week: the thing that keeps going. That's why many teachers, when someone has drifted, don't say all five tomorrow or don't bother.

teach.h: PRAY THE NEXT ONE. GUARD IT. ADD ONE.
teach.b: They say: pray the next one. Guard it. Then add another.

The goal stays five; the way back is one at a time. If there's a long stretch of missed prayers behind you, scholars differ on how to make them up; that's a question for a teacher you trust, not a reason to wait.
Then there's the voice that says you've already failed. Camp two named it: waswas, the whisper. One of its oldest tricks is telling a person the door has shut.

teach.h: COME WALKING, AND HE COMES RUNNING.
teach.b: A saying the Prophet reported from Allah, in Bukhari, says the opposite: whoever draws near to Me by a hand's span, I draw near by an arm's length; whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him running.
And it's fine to ask for help with the praying itself.
The Prophet told the companion Mu'adh that he loved him, then taught him to say at the end of every prayer: O Allah, help me to remember You, to thank You, and to worship You well.

how: Muslims hold the five daily prayers to be a duty; when someone has drifted from them, many imams and teachers advise coming back prayer by prayer, keeping each one steady, and asking a trusted scholar about making up what was missed.

o: the most constant deeds, even if small
the biggest deeds, done once with effort
the deeds done in secret, unseen by others

games.q: what's inside today — tap the pairs.
p: taught to ask for help to worship well

s: in the hadith, only big, heroic acts of worship are praised
the saying Aisha reported praises the most constant deeds, even if small.
mainstream teaching holds all five daily prayers to be a duty
the lesson says it plainly: the goal stays five; the way back is one at a time.
in a saying reported from Allah, the one who comes walking is met running
Bukhari reports it: whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him running.

games.q: you've missed a week of prayers. the next adhan sounds, and a voice says: you've already blown it, why bother? what does today's lesson point to?
o: wait until you can do all five perfectly
pray the next one, and guard it
games.why: pray the next one. the deeds most loved are the steady ones, even if small, and the goal stays five.

practice: If you pray, choose just the next prayer, the one coming, and decide only that one, not the whole week; if you've been away a while, picture making wudu for it, and let that be enough.
If you don't pray, choose one small good thing you once kept up and let slide, and picture doing it once more. Breathe out the guilt; breathe in the next one.

wordCard.voice: Adwamuha. The most constant of deeds, even if small: what the Prophet said Allah loves most.

orig.note: Arabic: even if it is little, from the saying adwamuha wa in qall, the most constant of them, even if small.

carryVoice: Your line: small, steady, and back again. The door hasn't shut. Day one hundred thirteen.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 6464 (the most beloved deeds to Allah are the most constant, even if small)
Sahih Muslim 783 (Aisha: when he did a deed, he kept it up)
Sahih al-Bukhari 7405 (hadith qudsi: a hand's span, an arm's length; walking, running)
Sunan Abi Dawud 1522 (Mu'adh: O Allah, help me to remember You, thank You and worship You well)
Qur'an 4:103 (prayer prescribed for believers at fixed times)
